newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela, Dutch Queen Beatrix toast new friendship.
newsitem.headline: Mandela, Dutch Queen Beatrix toast new friendship.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela and his dinner guest, Queen Beatrix of the Netherlands, said on Monday how sad they were that people of Dutch descent had concocted apartheid and how happy they were it was over.

"So many people in our country were appalled to see the Dutch word 'apartheid' become the symbol of the deep division in your country and the oppression of the majority of its people," Beatrix said at a state banquet in her honour in Pretoria.
She arrived in South Africa on Sunday with husband Prince Claus and son Prince Willem Alexander, heir to the throne, for the first visit by a Dutch head of state.

Mandela brought his daughter Zindzi to dinner, disappointing some socialite guests who said they had hoped to see Graca Machel, the new girlfriend he has slowly introduced to the public but has not yet invited to a major state occasion.

Beatrix's visit puts the symbolic royal seal of approval on reconciliation with the former colony which the Dutch shunned during four decades of apartheid (separateness), the official term for the failed ideology of racial segregation.
Mandela, who wore a black casual shirt, his trademark, won warm applause when he thanked the Netherlands for its support against the old apartheid regime that ended in 1994.

"The country from which the majority of European settlers in our country originated, from which the architects of apartheid were spawned, from which racists sought to draw succour, is a country that stood amongst the firmest against racism in South Afica," he said.
"Visitors to your country are deeply impressed by the absence of hatred and vengefulness among the great majority of the population," Beatrix, in a tiara and emerald green dress, said.
Earlier she inspected a ceremonial guard of honour at the Union Buildings in Pretoria, one of two traditional seats of parliament which currently sits only in Cape Town.
A sizeable business delegation is travelling with the queen.
The Netherlands now ranks ninth in the South African league table of foreign investment with total assets worth some $470 million.
After visiting some deprived townships during her tour of the Johannesburg area, Beatrix will head to Cape Town to end her four-day state visit. Then the royal family will stay on for a holiday.

The lush vineyards and gabled farmhouses fringing Cape Town's urban sprawl are present-day reminders of the city's origins as a refreshment station for 17th century Dutch mariners bound for the spice islands of the Indies.

The Dutch settled in the Cape more by chance than design after one of their ships was wrecked there. The proudly independent community absorbed German and French settlers and called themselves Afrikaners, the Dutch word for Africans.
For centuries they struggled against the British for white control of South Africa until the Afrikaner-led National Party won power after World War Two and began to construct apartheid.
The royal family of South Africa's other former colonial master, Britain, has also given its blessing to the new democracy that replaced apartheid two years ago. Queen Elizabeth visited last year.
On an informal trade visit in 1954, Beatrix's German-born father Prince Bernhard spoke out against apartheid.
In 1960 the Dutch government condemned apartheid after the Sharpeville massacre of 69 black demonstrators and over the next two decades it led international opposition to the white regime.
